name: Social Proof
description: People look to others' behavior (what most people actually do) to decide their own actions, especially under uncertainty.
design_relevance_note: Underlies '10,000 people bought this,' review counts, and 'trending now' UI patterns — genuinely effective, and also directly weaponizable as fake social-proof counters.
prevalence_note: One of the most-cited Cialdini principles in UX practice — review counts, 'X people bought this,' and testimonial placement are near-universal patterns.

findings.description: Social norms meaningfully affect behavior only once injunctive norms (what others approve/disapprove) and descriptive norms (what others actually do) are properly separated and one type is made salient; across 5 field settings, littering behavior changed in line with whichever norm type was focal.
findings.effect_size: Directional (behavior shifted per salient norm type across 5 field studies; no single pooled effect size reported)
findings.source_title: A Focus Theory of Normative Conduct: Recycling the Concept of Norms to Reduce Littering in Public Places
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: A credit union's social-proof spending intervention cut eating-out spending, but revealed people avoid seeing 'bad news' comparisons
applications.description: The Center for Advanced Hindsight ran a social-proof intervention with Arizona Federal Credit Union: 8,000 members were emailed an invitation to see how their eating-out spending compared to similar households (via anonymized data from Plaid). Members who completed the full experience and committed to a spending target spent about $17 less the following week than a control group. But the intervention also revealed a selection problem: people told they spent more than their peers dropped out of the experience at 58%, versus 35% for those told they spent the same or less.
applications.ethical_note: A genuinely honest case: the researchers disclosed that the intervention's apparent effectiveness may be confounded by who chose to see it through (people expecting bad news disproportionately dropped out), rather than presenting only the flattering headline result -- a real illustration that social-proof interventions can create their own selection bias, distinct from whether the underlying comparison message is honest.

applications.title: Airbnb's rejected social-proof statements on host signup
applications.description: Airbnb tested two social-proof-framed messages on its host-signup landing page -- one citing '39% of nearby listings are fully booked this week,' another emphasizing hosts from '180 countries' -- and rejected both variations rather than shipping either.
applications.ethical_note: This isn't a deception case -- there's no indication the 39% figure or the 180-countries claim was fabricated, unlike the Amazon/Booking.com entries elsewhere in this corpus. It's included specifically because it shows numeric social proof can backfire on its own terms even when honestly reported: a real, presumably accurate occupancy statistic reduced host confidence rather than building it, and a diversity statistic raised concern rather than reassurance. Worth pairing with entries that show social proof working, so this tier doesn't read as one-directional 'this technique always converts.'

applications.title: Etsy's 'In X carts' cart-count social proof message
applications.description: Etsy tested displaying how many other shoppers recently added a specific item to their cart (e.g. 'In 3 carts') in bold text on product pages, and appears to have kept a refined version of the message live and moved it higher on the page.
applications.ethical_note: 'X people have this in their cart' counters are a well-known pattern class scrutinized elsewhere for whether the number shown is genuinely live and accurate rather than inflated or static -- GoodUI's account here doesn't confirm or deny Etsy's specific implementation's accuracy, so this entry can't responsibly grade higher than 'mixed.' Worth flagging as an open question rather than either accusing Etsy of fabrication (no evidence found for that) or waving the pattern through as clean (the honesty of the underlying count is exactly what would need checking before calling it safe).

applications.title: Profile photos on a dating site's homepage decreased search activity
applications.description: A New Zealand dating site (findsomeone.co.nz) added general member profile photos to its homepage as a social-proof signal, and measured a decrease in search activity rather than an increase.
applications.ethical_note: Unlike the Amazon/Booking.com/Etsy entries in this corpus, there's no persuasion-tactic angle here at all -- displaying member photos isn't inherently manipulative, and the negative effect might even reflect users reasonably avoiding a mildly privacy-uncomfortable exposure (per the comment-thread speculation on the source page) rather than a UX failure. Graded not_applicable rather than 'unclear' (reserved for cases with a real but unresolved ethical dimension) -- this is included as a clean counter-example that social proof isn't a uniform lever, more than as an ethics case.

applications.title: Speero's eye-tracking study on which social-proof formats actually get noticed and remembered
applications.description: Speero (a CRO/experimentation agency) ran an eye-tracking and post-task-recall study comparing 8 different social-proof formats (testimonials, press-mention quotes, star ratings, etc.) plus a no-social-proof control on an e-commerce product page. All formats attracted attention at a similar speed (avg. 8.3 seconds to first fixation), but the three text-heavy formats (two testimonial styles and press-mention quotes) held attention far longer (avg. 1.06 seconds fixation time) than lighter-weight formats like star ratings -- and were also significantly more likely to be remembered afterward.
applications.ethical_note: This is genuinely useful methodological evidence for designers deciding how to present real social proof (which formats communicate real information most effectively), not a manipulation technique in itself -- no persuasion-vs-user-interest tension as long as the underlying testimonials/press mentions being displayed are themselves genuine.
